item.title: Practical Network Troubleshooting and Packet Flow Diagnostics in Linux Environments
item.description:
When inter-host communication is interrupted or intermittent timeouts occur in production infrastructure, haphazard service restarts or unplanned routing changes can expand the scope of the failure and result in the loss of volatile forensic evidence. Particularly in systems involving multi-NIC configurations or overlay networks, failure causes are complexly intertwined across physical links, OS kernel routing tables, host-based packet filtering, and the transport layer (TCP/UDP). This article outlines procedures for isolating network failures and packet tracing methods in Linux environments based on a deterministic and reproducible verification methodology.

💡 Hierarchical Approach to Localizing the Failure Domain

When detecting network anomalies, it is necessary to logically narrow down the investigation scope through bottom-up verification from lower layers (L1/L2) to upper layers (L7), or middle-out verification depending on the symptoms.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Standard Diagnostic Progression Flow |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1. Physical Link & NIC State |
| v |
| 2. Layer 3: IP Address & CIDR Subnet Alignment |
| v |
| 3. Layer 2/3: ARP Resolution & Next-Hop Gateway Reachability |
| v |
| 4. Routing Table & Egress Interface Selection |
| v |
| 5. Layer 4: TCP/UDP Port Listeners & Connection State Tracking |
| v |
| 6. Packet Filtering: Local, Host-Level, and Perimetric Firewalls |
| v |
| 7. Name Resolution: DNS Recursion & Query Path |
| v |
| 8. Layer 7: TLS Negotiation, HTTP Semantics & Application Upstreams |
| v |
| 9. Deep Packet Inspection: tcpdump Capture & Flow Trajectory Analysis |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

1. Verification of Interface Status and Layer 3 Address Configurations

When a communication failure occurs, first verify the physical carrier status of the Network Interface Controller (NIC) and the assigned IP/subnet mask.

ip -br link
ip link show ens160
ethtool ens160

If the status is DOWN in ip -br link or if Link detected: no appears in the ethtool output, an issue exists in the hypervisor virtual switch port group, VLAN tag, or physical layer cabling.

ip -br addr

Special attention must be paid to misconfigurations of the subnet mask (CIDR prefix). If a setting that should be /24 is accidentally defined as /16, traffic destined for non-adjacent segments is treated as directly connected (Link Scope). Consequently, ARP requests are broadcast locally without passing through the default gateway, causing packets to fail to reach their destination and be dropped.

2. Verification of Kernel Routing Table and ARP Resolution

To identify which interface a packet is egressed through from the source node, query the kernel’s forwarding decision directly.

ip route
ip route get 192.168.20.50

From the execution results, accurately determine the selected next-hop gateway (via), egress interface (dev), and source IP address (src). In multi-homed configurations equipped with multiple NICs, asymmetric routing may cause return packets to take a different path and be dropped by an intermediate stateful firewall.

Next, verify whether the Layer 2 address of the next hop is resolved.

ip neigh show

If the status is INCOMPLETE or FAILED, no response to the ARP request has been received. VLAN misconfiguration on the switch side, physical communication disruption, or IP address conflicts should be suspected.

3. Layer 4 Socket Listener and Protocol Isolation

Even if ICMP reachability via ping succeeds, it does not guarantee that TCP/UDP application communication will be established. This is because ICMP (Echo Request/Reply) lacks the concept of transport layer ports.

To confirm port reachability from a client, execute nc (netcat) with a specified timeout.

nc -zv -w 3 192.168.20.50 443

On the server side, verify whether the socket is listening on the intended interface and port.

sudo ss -lntp

If the bind address is restricted to loopback, such as 127.0.0.1:8080, all incoming traffic from external nodes will be rejected by the kernel (TCP RST). Daemons requiring external access must be bound to 0.0.0.0 or the specific address of a physical NIC.

4. Verification of Packet Filtering (nftables / firewalld)

If communication fails even when the socket is properly in a listening state, inspect the host-level packet filter.

sudo firewall-cmd --state
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
sudo nft list ruleset

When inspecting filter configurations, thoroughly check interface zones, source IP restrictions, and protocol port allow rules based on infrastructure design, rather than merely verifying daemon running status.

🛠️ Packet Capture and Flow Analysis Using tcpdump

When static checks using various commands cannot identify the cause, use tcpdump to capture frames passing through the network interface directly.

sudo tcpdump -nn -i ens160 'host 192.168.20.50 and tcp port 443'

-nn`: Disables host name resolution and port service name resolution to prevent name resolution delays.

  • -i ens160: Specifies the capture target interface.
  • 'host ... and tcp port ...': Filters traffic using BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter).

When outputting PCAP files for detailed analysis, specify a packet count limit and manage appropriate permissions.

sudo tcpdump -nn -i ens160 -s 0 -c 1000 -w /tmp/network-debug.pcap 'host 192.168.20.50 and tcp port 443'
sudo chmod 600 /tmp/network-debug.pcap

Identifying Failure Causes via TCP Handshake Signatures 

Client (192.168.10.10) Server (192.168.20.50)
 | |
 |-------------- [SYN] Seq=0 ------------------>| Step 1: Connection Request
 | |
 |<--------- [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1 ------------| Step 2: Acknowledgment & Sync
 | |
 |-------------- [ACK] Seq=1 Ack=1 ------------>| Step 3: Handshake Established
 | |
 |========= Established / Data Transfer ========|

The location of a bottleneck can be identified through TCP flag transitions in the capture log.

Pattern 1: SYN Retransmission and Silent Drop (No Response) 

192.168.10.10.52000 > 192.168.20.50.443: Flags [S], seq 1001, win 64240, length 0
192.168.10.10.52000 > 192.168.20.50.443: Flags [S], seq 1001, win 64240, length 0

If Flags [S] is transmitted from the client but no response is received, drops by intermediate network firewalls (cloud Security Groups, NACLs, etc.), routing blackholes, or lost return packets due to asymmetric routing should be suspected.

Pattern 2: Immediate TCP RST (Connection Refused) 

192.168.10.10.52000 > 192.168.20.50.443: Flags [S], seq 1001, length 0
192.168.20.50.443 > 192.168.10.10.52000: Flags [R.], seq 0, ack 1002, length 0

If Flags [R.] is returned immediately from the target host, it indicates that the packet reached the destination host, but no process is listening on the relevant port, the OS connection backlog queue is exhausted, or the packet filter returned an explicit REJECT (–reject-with tcp-reset).

Pattern 3: Stalling After Handshake Completion

If data communication stalls after Flags [S], Flags [S.], and Flags [.] are successfully established, there is no issue with Layer 4 reachability; the cause lies in a TLS handshake mismatch (SNI configuration or certificate revocation) or a communication failure between a Layer 7 proxy (such as Nginx) and the backend.

⚠️ Troubleshooting

The handling procedures for common scenarios encountered in actual troubleshooting sites are shown below.

1. HTTP 502 Bad Gateway Occurrence and Upstream Connection Diagnostics

This occurs when traffic reaches the reverse proxy from the client, but the connection from the proxy to the backend (such as a FastAPI or Go application) is severed.

# Check the backend listener from the proxy server
nc -zv -w 3 127.0.0.1 8000
sudo ss -lntp | grep ':8000'

# Inspect backend process status and logs
sudo journalctl -u backend-service --since "10 minutes ago"
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log

If connect() failed (111: Connection refused) is recorded in the Nginx error log, either the backend process is down or a bind address mismatch (discrepancy between IPv6 [::1] and IPv4 127.0.0.1) has occurred. In the case of upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out), the cause is backend processing deadlock or database-induced latency.

2. Hardware Offload Artifacts During Capture

When TSO (TCP Segmentation Offload) or TX Checksum Offload is enabled on the NIC, checksum errors or giant packets exceeding MTU (1500 bytes) may be observed in tcpdump. This is an apparent artifact resulting from capturing packets immediately after the kernel offloads frame processing to the NIC, and does not indicate packet corruption. To verify the accurate state of actual frames, packet capture must be performed on the receiving host or via a network tap.

Log Data

Representative terminal output examples obtained during diagnostics at each layer are shown below.

$ ip -br link
lo UNKNOWN 00:00:00:00:00:00 <loopback,up,lower_up> 
ens160 UP 00:50:56:bb:01:1a <broadcast,multicast,up,lower_up> 
ens192 DOWN 00:50:56:bb:02:2b <broadcast,multicast> 

$ ip route get 192.168.20.50
192.168.20.50 via 192.168.10.1 dev ens160 src 192.168.10.10 uid 1000
 cache 

$ ip neigh show
192.168.10.1 dev ens160 lladdr 00:11:22:33:44:55 REACHABLE

$ sudo ss -lntp
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:PortProcess
LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:22 0.0.0.0:* users:(("sshd",pid=1024,fd=3))
LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:8080 0.0.0.0:* users:(("java",pid=2450,fd=45))
LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:443 0.0.0.0:* users:(("nginx",pid=1820,fd=6))

$ nc -zv -w 3 192.168.20.50 443
Ncat: Version 7.92 ( https://nmap.org/ncat )
Ncat: Connected to 192.168.20.50:443.
Ncat: 0 bytes sent, 0 bytes received in 0.02 seconds.

🛠️ Operational Notes

When performing network analysis on hosts running in production environments, the following constraints must be adhered to:

  1. Strict BPF Filtering: Executing unconditional tcpdump in high-traffic environments can cause high CPU utilization and log space exhaustion. Always specify IP and port, and limit the captured packet count using the -c option.
  2. Preservation of Volatile Information: Before modifying network settings or rebooting, record the output of ip route, ip neigh, and ss to preserve state information at the time of the failure.
  3. Rigorous Layer Separation: Rather than determining path viability solely by Ping success or failure, individually isolating L3 (routing), L4 (port/socket), and L7 (application protocol) is the fastest route to incident recovery.</broadcast,multicast></broadcast,multicast,up,lower_up></loopback,up,lower_up>

item.title: Troubleshooting the Boundary Area Where Ping Succeeds but TCP Connection Fails
item.description:
In infrastructure operations, the issue where “Ping succeeds, but connections to the server (such as SSH or HTTP) fail” frequently occurs. Relying solely on ICMP for L3-level reachability verification while neglecting the verification of L4 transport layer or L7 application layer leads to delayed incident recovery and incorrect root cause identification.

The ICMP echo test indicates a successful state with low latency and 0% packet loss.

$ ping 192.168.10.100
PING 192.168.10.100 (192.168.10.100) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 192.168.10.100: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.3 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.10.100: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.2 ms

However, initiating an SSH session or HTTP request results in a connection failure.

$ ssh 192.168.10.100
ssh: connect to host 192.168.10.100 port 22: Connection refused

Alternatively, a timeout occurs during the connection attempt.

$ curl http://192.168.10.100:8080
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 192.168.10.100 port 8080: Connection timed out

The assumption that “since Ping succeeded, the network is normal, and connection failure means the server itself is broken” is technically incorrect. This is because ICMP operates at the network layer (L3), whereas key application protocols such as SSH, HTTP, HTTPS, PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Redis rely on transport layer (L4) TCP sockets bound to specific port numbers.

This article systematically breaks down this boundary gap and establishes diagnostic methodologies centered on three core Linux utilities: ss, nc, and tcpdump.

1. Network Layer Abstraction and Service Mapping

💡 To effectively identify communication bottlenecks, target services are mapped to each layer of the OSI reference model and transport mechanisms.

  • ICMP: Used exclusively for diagnostic and control messaging such as ping (no transport port exists).
  • SSH: TCP port 22
  • HTTP: TCP port 80
  • HTTPS: TCP port 443
  • PostgreSQL: TCP port 5432
  • MySQL / MariaDB: TCP port 3306
  • Redis: TCP port 6379

Because ICMP operates independently of L4 TCP listening sockets, receiving a response to an ICMP Echo Request provides no guarantee that a TCP port is open or reachable.

2. Low-Layer Mechanics of ping

Executing ping 192.168.10.100 sends an ICMP Echo Request packet (Type 8) to the destination host, which returns an ICMP Echo Reply packet (Type 0).

+------------------------+ +------------------------+
| Client: 192.168.10.50 | | Server: 192.168.10.100 |
+------------------------+ +------------------------+
 | |
 |------------ ICMP Echo Request (Type 8) ------------->|
 | |
 |<----------- ICMP Echo Reply (Type 0) ----------------|
 | |

A successful Ping merely confirms that the path from the client through local routing, gateways, the physical network, and the target IP stack back to the ICMP reply is functional. It cannot verify whether firewall rules allow TCP frames or whether an application daemon on the host is actively processing sockets.

3. Structure of the TCP 3-Way Handshake

When initiating a TCP-based service connection, the operating system kernel must first establish a stateful connection via the TCP 3-Way Handshake.

Client (192.168.10.50) Server (192.168.10.100:22)
 | |
 |----------------------- 1. SYN ------------------------------>|
 | |
 |<------------------- 2. SYN-ACK ------------------------------|
 | |
 |----------------------- 3. ACK ------------------------------>|
 | |
[ ESTABLISHED ] [ ESTABLISHED ]
  1. SYN: The client sends a TCP frame with the SYN flag set to request connection initiation.
  2. SYN-ACK: Upon receiving the SYN, the server checks the socket listening on port 22, allocates a connection state buffer, and responds with SYN-ACK.
  3. ACK: The client responds with ACK, and both endpoints transition to the ESTABLISHED state.

For application protocols to function, this L4 sequence must complete successfully.

4. Diagnosing “Ping Succeeds + TCP Connection Fails”

Define the initial diagnostic state.

$ ping 192.168.10.100
# Success (0% packet loss)

$ nc -zv 192.168.10.100 22
# Failure

This discrepancy allows immediate narrowing down of the failure domain. Functional ICMP indicates that L3 routing and physical links are operational, while TCP failure indicates an issue with L4 sockets, firewalls, or service daemons.

5. Transport Layer Probing with nc (Netcat)

Netcat (nc) functions as a TCP and UDP connection analyzer. Its primary use case in production environments is verifying raw TCP reachability to a specific socket address.

To run Netcat, specify options for port scanning.

$ nc -zv 192.168.10.100 22

-z`: Zero-I/O mode (scans for listening daemons without sending payload data).

  • -v: Verbose output mode.

Determine network status from connection test execution results.

  1. Handshake Success:

    Connection to 192.168.10.100 22 port [tcp/ssh] succeeded!

  2. Failure Pattern A:

    nc: connect to 192.168.10.100 port 22 failed: Connection refused

  3. Failure Pattern B:

    nc: connect to 192.168.10.100 port 22 failed: Connection timed out

Understanding the distinction between Connection Refused and Connection Timed Out is critical in identifying root causes.

6. Mechanisms of Connection Refused and Connection Timeout

Mechanics of Connection Refused

⚠️ A Connection refused error indicates that the client’s SYN packet reached the destination host’s kernel, but the host explicitly rejected the connection and returned a TCP Reset (RST) frame.

Client Server
 | |
 |--------------------------- SYN ---------------------------->| (Destination host reached)
 | | (No listening process)
 |<------------------------ TCP RST ---------------------------|

Primary Causes:

  1. Service Daemon Stopped: The process (sshd, nginx, mysqld, etc.) is not running.
  2. Incorrect Service Port: The application is listening on a non-default port (e.g., 2222 instead of 22).
  3. Bound Interface Mismatch: The daemon is bound strictly to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0.
  4. Active Packet Filtering: The localhost firewall is configured to explicitly return TCP Reset packets (REJECT) rather than dropping them (DROP).

Mechanics of Connection Timeout

A Connection timed out error occurs when the client sends a SYN packet, but no response whatsoever is returned before the socket timeout threshold expires.

Client Network / Firewall / Target
 | |
 |--------------------------- SYN ---------------------------->|
 | | ===> [ Drop / Block ]
 | (No Response) |
 | ... Timeout ... |

Primary Causes:

  1. Network Security Drop: Cloud security groups, network ACLs, or hardware firewalls are silently dropping inbound traffic.
  2. Host-Level Firewall Drop: iptables, firewalld, or nftables are configured with a DROP action.
  3. Routing Failure: Incorrect default routing or missing static routes at intermediate network switches or routers.
  4. Asymmetric Routing / Return Path Failure: The server receives the SYN and sends a SYN-ACK, but the packet is dropped or misrouted on the return path.

7. Inspecting Local Sockets with ss

The ss (Socket Statistics) utility inspects active internal sockets on Linux platforms and serves as a modern replacement for the legacy netstat tool.

Run the diagnostic command to check socket state.

$ sudo ss -lntp

Flag Specifications:

  • -l: Displays only listening (LISTEN) sockets.
  • -n: Displays numeric addresses and ports (prevents overhead from DNS and service name resolution).
  • -t: Displays TCP sockets.
  • -p: Displays process IDs and names associated with sockets (requires root or sudo privileges).

Executing the command outputs socket information.

State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port Process
LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:22 0.0.0.0:* users:(("sshd",pid=1234,fd=3))
LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("nginx",pid=1500,fd=6))
LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:8080 0.0.0.0:* users:(("java",pid=2000,fd=20))

8. Analyzing Bind Addresses: 127.0.0.1 vs 0.0.0.0

The Local Address:Port bind configuration dictates external reachability.

Loopback Isolation Case (127.0.0.1:8080)

Indicates a state where the socket is bound exclusively to the loopback address.

LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:8080 0.0.0.0:*

The application process (java) is bound exclusively to the loopback interface (lo).

[ External Client ] [ Target Server ]
 192.168.10.50 192.168.10.100
 | |
 |--- HTTP request to 192.168.10.100:8080 --------->| [ Physical Interface ]
 | |
 | (Blocked / No socket)
 | v
 | [ Loopback Interface ]
 | 127.0.0.1:8080 (Java Daemon)

Local Verification: Executing curl http://127.0.0.1:8080 on the server succeeds.

  • Remote Verification: Executing curl http://192.168.10.100:8080 from an external client fails.

Wildcard IPv4 Bind (0.0.0.0:8080)

Indicates a state where the socket is bound across all interfaces.

LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:8080 0.0.0.0:*

The socket accepts inbound TCP traffic through all active IPv4 network interfaces assigned to the host (e.g., ens160 with IP 192.168.10.100). If permitted by firewalls, connections from external clients are possible.

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Server: 192.168.10.100 |
| |
| Interface ens160 [ 192.168.10.100 ] <--- [ External Request ] |
| | |
| v |
| Service bound to 0.0.0.0:8080 (Listening on all interfaces) |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

9. Real-World Troubleshooting Cases

Case 1: Ping Succeeds, but SSH Fails (Connection Refused)

Environment Configuration:

  • Client: 192.168.10.50
  • Server: 192.168.10.100
  • Target Service: SSH (TCP port 22)

Step 1: Client-Side Diagnostics 

$ ping 192.168.10.100
# Result: 64 bytes from 192.168.10.100: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.3 ms (Success)

$ nc -zv 192.168.10.100 22
# Result: nc: connect to 192.168.10.100 port 22 failed: Connection refused

Step 2: Server-Side Socket Inspection

Log in to the server’s local console or out-of-band (OOB) management interface.

$ sudo ss -lntp
# Output result:
# LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("nginx",pid=1500,fd=6))

TCP port 22 is absent from the listener table.

Step 3: Verifying Service State and Resolution 

$ sudo systemctl status sshd
# Output: Active: inactive (dead)

$ sudo systemctl start sshd
$ sudo systemctl enable sshd

$ sudo ss -lntp | grep ':22'
# Output: LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:22 0.0.0.0:* users:(("sshd",pid=3102,fd=3))

Re-executing nc -zv 192.168.10.100 22 on the client side results in a successful connection.

Case 2: Process Running, but External Access Fails (Bind Mismatch)

Diagnostic State:

Executing ss -lntp on the application server yields the socket state.

LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:8080 0.0.0.0:* users:(("node",pid=4211,fd=18))

Reachability Testing:

  • From Target Server: curl http://127.0.0.1:8080 $\longrightarrow$ 200 OK
  • From Remote Client: curl http://192.168.10.100:8080 $\longrightarrow$ Connection Refused

Diagnostics and Solution:

The application (Node.js, Spring Boot, Nginx, etc.) configuration is restricted to localhost. Modify the host configuration (e.g., server.host = 0.0.0.0 or LISTEN 0.0.0.0:8080) and restart the service to expose the socket to external interfaces.

Case 3: Service Bound, but External Connection Times Out

Diagnostic State:

The server’s socket table is properly exposed.

$ sudo ss -lntp | grep ':8080'
LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:8080 0.0.0.0:* users:(("java",pid=8820,fd=7))

However, client-side execution fails.

$ nc -zv 192.168.10.100 8080
nc: connect to 192.168.10.100 port 8080 failed: Connection timed out

Firewall Inspection:

Because the output is Timeout rather than Refused, an inline network device or host firewall rule is silently dropping packets.

Inspect localhost rules.

$ sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
# Check if '8080/tcp' exists in the services and ports section

$ sudo nft list ruleset

If ICMP is globally permitted in firewalld but port 8080 is excluded, ping passes through while L4 TCP traffic to port 8080 is dropped.

Client (192.168.10.50) Server (192.168.10.100)
 | |
 |----------------------- TCP SYN ---------------------------->|
 | |
 | [ Host Firewall (nftables) ]
 | [ Action: DROP Port 8080 ]
 | |
 | <=== Timeout (SYN-ACK is not sent) =========================|

10. Deep Packet Diagnostics with tcpdump

nc reports connection results, and ss indicates socket listening state. However, tcpdump captures actual packet movement and reveals state transitions at the frame level.

Run packet capture on the target server.

$ sudo tcpdump -nn -i ens160 tcp port 8080

-n`: Do not resolve hostnames.

  • -nn: Do not resolve hostnames or port names (displays numeric IPs and ports).
  • -i ens160: Monitors traffic on target network interface ens160.
  • tcp port 8080: Filters strictly TCP packets passing through port 8080.

11. Packet Pattern Analysis with tcpdump

Scenario A: Normal TCP 3-Way Handshake 

10:00:01.001 IP 192.168.10.50.52344 > 192.168.10.100.8080: Flags [S], seq 1001
10:00:01.002 IP 192.168.10.100.8080 > 192.168.10.50.52344: Flags [S.], seq 2001, ack 1002
10:00:01.003 IP 192.168.10.50.52344 > 192.168.10.100.8080: Flags [.], seq 1002, ack 2002

Flags [S]`: Initial SYN frame from client.

  • Flags [S.]: SYN-ACK response from server.
  • Flags [.]: ACK frame from client.
  • Diagnosis: L4 handshake completed and connection established (ESTABLISHED).

Scenario B: Sustained Unanswered Inbound SYN 

10:00:01.001 IP 192.168.10.50.52344 > 192.168.10.100.8080: Flags [S], seq 1001
10:00:04.005 IP 192.168.10.50.52344 > 192.168.10.100.8080: Flags [S], seq 1001
10:00:10.009 IP 192.168.10.50.52344 > 192.168.10.100.8080: Flags [S], seq 1001

Observation: The client is retransmitting TCP SYN. The server’s interface receives the packet, but no outbound SYN-ACK ([S.]) is sent.

  • Diagnosis: A host-level security mechanism (iptables, nftables, SELinux, or kernel-level IP filtering) drops the packet immediately upon ingress at the network interface layer.

Scenario C: Server Sends SYN-ACK, but Client Retransmits SYN 

10:00:01.001 IP 192.168.10.50.52344 > 192.168.10.100.8080: Flags [S]
10:00:01.002 IP 192.168.10.100.8080 > 192.168.10.50.52344: Flags [S.]
10:00:04.005 IP 192.168.10.50.52344 > 192.168.10.100.8080: Flags [S]

Observation: The server processes inbound SYN and transmits SYN-ACK, but the client continuously sends SYN frames as if no response was received.

  • Diagnosis: A return path routing failure between server and client, or egress firewall filtering toward the source direction, is occurring.
Client (192.168.10.50) Server (192.168.10.100)
 | |
 |----------------------- 1. SYN ----------------------------->|
 | |
 | X <=== [ Return routing failure / Egress block ] ---------| (Sending SYN-ACK)

Primary causes:

  1. Misconfigured local default gateway on the target server.
  2. Return path drops due to asymmetric routing policies.
  3. Loss of NAT table state.

Scenario D: Immediate Reset (RST Immediately Following SYN) 

10:00:01.001 IP 192.168.10.50.52344 > 192.168.10.100.8080: Flags [S]
10:00:01.001 IP 192.168.10.100.8080 > 192.168.10.50.52344: Flags [R.]

Observation: The server immediately returns a reset frame ([R.]).

  • Diagnosis: The packet passed through the host firewall, but the kernel found no process listening on TCP port 8080. Verify daemon status with ss -lntp.

12. Tracking Socket State via Kernel Counters

Run ss -ant to review connection state allocation across active sockets.

$ sudo ss -ant
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port
LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:8080 0.0.0.0:*
ESTAB 0 0 192.168.10.100:8080 192.168.10.50:52344
SYN-RECV 0 0 192.168.10.100:8080 192.168.10.50:52345

Critical Socket States and Anomalies:

  1. Accumulation of SYN-SENT (Client Side):

    $ ss -ant state syn-sent

Meaning*: The client application transmitted a SYN frame but has not received a SYN-ACK. Indicates outbound blocking or drop along the path.

  1. Accumulation of SYN-RECV (Server Side):

    $ ss -ant state syn-recv

Meaning*: The server received SYN and transmitted SYN-ACK, but remains stalled waiting for the final ACK from the client. Indicates inbound blocking on the client side, asymmetric routing, or a SYN flood attack.

13. Upper-Layer Diagnostics: Ping and TCP Succeed, but Application Fails

Define a further elevated failure state.

$ ping 192.168.10.100
# Success (L3 OK)

$ nc -zv 192.168.10.100 8080
# Success (L4 TCP connection OK)

$ curl http://192.168.10.100:8080/
# Failure / Error / HTTP 5xx / No response

This scenario proves that the network layer (L3) and transport layer (L4) are fully operational.

Application Layer Debugging with curl

Execute verbose HTTP operations to capture handshake and protocol semantics.

$ curl -v http://192.168.10.100:8080/

Example of a verbose execution trace:

* Trying 192.168.10.100:8080...
* Connected to 192.168.10.100 (192.168.10.100) port 8080 (#0)
> GET / HTTP/1.1
> Host: 192.168.10.100:8080
> User-Agent: curl/7.76.1
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.1 504 Gateway Timeout
< Server: nginx/1.20.1
< Date: Mon, 10 Nov 2025 10:00:00 GMT
< Content-Type: text/html

Primary Cause Categories for L7 Failures:

  1. Reverse Proxy Upstream Timeout: Nginx accepts connections on port 8080, but fails to reach the backend running locally (e.g., Node/Java app on 127.0.0.1:8000), returning HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout or 502 Bad Gateway.
  2. HTTP Host Header Rejection: Application virtual host filters drop requests lacking a valid Host: request header.
  3. Application Thread Lock: Database connection pool exhaustion or internal deadlocks prevent the application layer from transmitting payload frames despite an established L4 socket handshake.
  4. TLS/SSL Handshake Failure: Cipher suite mismatches, expired certificates, or SNI misconfigurations cause connection termination immediately following TCP initialization on port 443.

14. Caveats in UDP Protocol Diagnostics

Unlike TCP, UDP is connectionless. There are no setup flags (SYN, ACK) or state machine checks.

Testing UDP reachability using nc requires the -u flag.

$ nc -zvu 192.168.10.100 53

Diagnostic Challenges:

  • UDP scanners transmit 0-byte packets. If no ICMP Port Unreachable frame returns, nc determines the port to be “open” or “open|filtered”.
  • Due to a high rate of false positives, reliable UDP testing requires protocol-specific query tools (e.g., dig for DNS UDP 53, snmpwalk for SNMP UDP 161) alongside active packet capture.
$ sudo tcpdump -nn -i ens160 udp port 53

17. Operational CLI Quick Reference

L3 Diagnostic Commands: 

# Send 4 ICMP packets to test link reachability
$ ping -c 4 192.168.10.100

L4 Socket Probing Commands (nc): 

# Investigate standard management and web service TCP ports
$ nc -zv 192.168.10.100 22
$ nc -zv 192.168.10.100 80
$ nc -zv 192.168.10.100 443
$ nc -zv 192.168.10.100 8080

# Investigate UDP domain name resolution service
$ nc -zvu 192.168.10.100 53

Local Socket Inspection Commands (ss): 

# List all active listening TCP ports including process details
$ sudo ss -lntp

# Filter for a specific target socket listener
$ sudo ss -lntp | grep ':8080'

# Display all numeric TCP connections regardless of state
$ sudo ss -ant

# Isolate connections in SYN-SENT or SYN-RECV state
$ sudo ss -ant state syn-sent
$ sudo ss -ant state syn-recv

Packet Analysis Commands (tcpdump): 

# Monitor TCP port 8080 on a specific interface
$ sudo tcpdump -nn -i ens160 tcp port 8080

# Capture raw SYN connection initialization requests globally
$ sudo tcpdump -nn -i ens160 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'

# Capture all traffic associated with a specific host IP address
$ sudo tcpdump -nn -i ens160 host 192.168.10.50

# Multiplex tracking of ICMP control packets and target TCP application traffic
$ sudo tcpdump -nn -i ens160 'tcp port 8080 or icmp'

Host Firewall Operations (firewalld / nftables): 

# Inspect current firewalld configuration
$ sudo firewall-cmd --list-all

# Permanently add permission for TCP 8080
$ sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent
$ sudo firewall-cmd --reload

# Inspect low-level nftables ruleset bindings
$ sudo nft list ruleset

Lessons Learned

  1. Ping Success Does Not Guarantee Service Health: ICMP Echo replies prove only Layer 3 interface reachability and routing functionality. Layer 4 port states and Layer 7 application functionality are not verified.
  2. Accurate Error Message Interpretation:
  • Connection refused indicates that the packet reached the host, but there is no active listener, or it was explicitly rejected with a RST. Check host socket bindings (ss -lntp).
  • Connection timed out indicates that frames were lost on the forward or return path. Check firewalls, security groups, and routing loops.
  1. Packet Path Tracing via Wire Capture: Use tcpdump to answer the fundamental question: “How far into the infrastructure stack did the initial SYN frame reach?”
  2. Step-by-Step Layer Isolation: Sequentially test from L3 (ping) to L4 (nc), inspect local listening states (ss), verify raw frames on the wire (tcpdump), and finally validate at L7 (curl).</server_ip>
